text: If only you were my brother, nursed at my mother's breast! Then I could kiss you when I found you in the street, and no one would despise me for it.
I would lead you and bring you to my mother's house — she would teach me — and I would give you spiced wine to drink, the juice of my pomegranates.
His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me.
I charge you, daughters of Jerusalem: do not stir up, do not awaken love until it desires.
Who is this coming up from the wilderness, leaning on the one she loves? Under the apple tree I awakened you; there your mother was in labor with you, there she who bore you brought you forth.

versions.text: Who is this coming up from the wilderness, leaning on the one she loves? Under the apple tree I awakened you; there your mother conceived you, there she who bore you was in labor.
versions.explanation: The verb חבל in both clauses refers to labor pains, not conception. Rendering the first occurrence as "conceived" weakens the parallelism and introduces a meaning the Hebrew does not carry.

text: Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm; for love is as strong as death, its passion as unyielding as the grave. Its flashes are flashes of fire, a flame of the LORD.
Many waters cannot quench love, nor can rivers wash it away. If a man offered all the wealth of his house for love, he would be utterly scorned.

versions.text: Many waters cannot quench love, nor can rivers wash it away. If a man offered all the wealth of his house for love, it would be utterly scorned.
versions.explanation: The pronoun לוֹ most naturally refers back to the man (אִישׁ), and this also echoes the same verb used of the speaker in verse 1 ("no one would despise me"). "He would be utterly scorned" keeps that link audible.

text: We have a little sister, and her breasts are not yet grown. What shall we do for our sister on the day she is spoken for?
If she is a wall, we will build turrets of silver upon her; if she is a door, we will enclose her with panels of cedar.
I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers. So in his eyes I have become as one who finds peace.

versions.text: I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers. So in his eyes I have become one who brings peace.
versions.explanation: The participle מוֹצְאֵת is active "one who finds," not "one who brings." The bride finds peace (or favor) in his sight; the current wording reverses the direction of the action.

text: Solomon had a vineyard at Baal-hamon. He leased the vineyard to caretakers; each was to bring for its fruit a thousand pieces of silver.
My own vineyard is before me. The thousand is yours, Solomon, and two hundred for those who tend its fruit.
You who dwell in the gardens, companions are listening for your voice — let me hear it!

versions.text: You who dwell in the gardens, my companions are listening for your voice — let me hear it!
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has no possessive pronoun on חֲבֵרִים; "my companions" adds content and narrows the sense. The bare plural reads just as smoothly aloud.

text: Hurry away, my beloved! Be like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of spices.

versions.text: Hurry, my beloved! Be like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of spices.
versions.explanation: בְּרַח carries the sense of hastening away or fleeing, which fits the following image of the gazelle bounding off to the mountains. "Hurry" alone loses the direction of movement.
